settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: README lines 21-33 show the documented usage registers a DenyAll GroovyValueFilter before evaluating, implying the intended contract is 'always register an interceptor'.
GroovyInterceptor javadoc (lines 146-153) states that interceptors block calls by throwing; this is the designed enforcement mechanism.
No interceptor implementation is in the read set, so it cannot be shown that a real embedder leaves the chain empty.
candidates.description: All Checker.checked* entry points build an invoker chain and, when the chain has no next interceptor, directly perform the underlying Groovy operation rather than denying it: checkedCall calls fakeCallSite(method).call(receiver,args) (line 157), checkedStaticCall calls fakeCallSite(method).callStatic((Class)receiver,args) (line 188), checkedConstructor calls fakeCallSite("<init>").callConstructor((Class)receiver,args) (line 200), checkedGetProperty/checkedSetProperty/checkedGetAttribute/checkedSetAttribute call ScriptBytecodeAdapter.getProperty/setProperty/getField/setField directly (lines 290, 347, 372, 406), and checkedGetArray/checkedSetArray call the fake "getAt"/"putAt" call sites (lines 422, 447). The comment at lines 149-151 explains that this fake-call-site path is the intended fallback. The safety of the whole design therefore rests entirely on the embedder having registered a strict interceptor in the current thread before executing the script; if registration is forgotten, misses a specific callback, or the interceptor only overrides a subset of the on* methods (GroovyInterceptor's defaults at lines 22-141 all forward the call unchanged), the sandboxed operation proceeds with no denial anywhere in the read code. This is a fail-open design rather than a defense-in-depth default-deny. Precondition is a host that invokes Checker without a fully restrictive interceptor; no such host configuration is present in the read set, so this is a design observation about the enforcement layer, not a demonstrated bypass.
missing_evidence: How workflow/embedding hosts register interceptors and whether any callback path can leave the chain empty for a dangerous operation.
Whether fakeCallSite() can succeed for operations that the interceptor normally blocks (i.e., which operations are safe to fall through unchecked).
preconditions: A caller compiles code with SandboxTransformer but does not register a GroovyInterceptor, or registers one whose overrides forward without denying.
Script reaches any Checker.checked* method with an empty interceptor chain.
candidates.title: Checker falls through to executing the raw operation when no interceptor is registered (no default deny)

counter_evidence: The transformer does rewrite the main taint conduits: MethodCallExpression, StaticMethodCallExpression, ConstructorCallExpression, PropertyExpression, AttributeExpression, array index, casts, and binary operators (lines 347-604).
Comments at lines 85-92 document the stated interception coverage, suggesting the exclusions are known and accepted by the author.
FieldExpression LHS and this/super constructor calls are Java bytecode constraints acknowledged in comments (lines 109-110, 513-515).
candidates.description: Enforcement happens by rewriting expressions in innerTransform. Constructs the transformer deliberately leaves alone are executed unchecked: instanceof (SandboxTransformer.java lines 538-539), logical operators (lines 541-542), FieldExpression on the LHS of an assignment (lines 512-516, with the comment that it is 'not sure how we can intercept this, so skipping this for now'), and special constructor calls this(...)/super(...) (lines 410-412). Additionally whole categories only occur when their boolean flag is enabled (interceptMethodCall, interceptConstructor, interceptProperty, interceptArray, interceptAttribute at lines 105-124); if a flag is turned off each corresponding `if (... && interceptXxx)` is skipped and super.transform(exp) is used, leaving the operation unchecked. Because the checks are attached to specific AST node types at the CANONICALIZATION phase (constructor at line 127), anything Groovy or an AST transformation generates after this phase, or any expression form not handled in innerTransform, is not routed through Checker. Runtime property/method lookup that bypasses the rewritten AST shape (e.g. MetaClass-driven dispatch, closures, dynamic construction) therefore has no Checker boundary to cross; this is a structural property of the design visible in the read source.
missing_evidence: A concrete script construct that demonstrably reaches an unguarded operation; none was constructed or executed.
Behaviour after CANONICALIZATION of Groovy-generated or AST-transformation-generated calls.
preconditions: Untrusted script uses an expression form not rewritten by innerTransform, or the embedder disables one of the interceptXxx flags.
Any Groovy/compiler path produces a call or field access that is not represented by the rewritten AST node at CANONICALIZATION time.
candidates.title: Interception is AST-rewriting only; unrewritten constructs and compiler-materialised calls escape checking

counter_evidence: ScopeTrackingClassCodeExpressionTransformer overrides visitMethod, visitField, visitBlockStatement, visitDoWhileLoop, visitForLoop, and visitIfElse to push scopes, covering common cases (lines 40-116).
The author documents the hack and flags it as fragile, indicating awareness; the read source does not prove a concrete mis-resolution.
No scope-tracking body beyond line 120 and no StackVariableSet source were read, so the tracker's completeness was not examined.
candidates.description: To decide whether `foo` is a local variable or an implicit-this property access, the transformer relies on a compile-time variable-scope tracker and a `visitingClosureBody` flag. Lines 355-358 and 681-687 route implicit-this calls inside a closure to the hacky CLOSURE_THIS expression, described in the source as 'a hack ... asWritable().getOwner()' (lines 767-778) that is 'subject to the method resolution rule' (line 262). Lines 436-449 and 467-481 treat any name found by isLocalVariable(...) as a local and hand it to super.transform unmodified. isLocalVariable is implemented as varScope.has(name) over a StackVariableSet built by the visitor, so correctness depends on every visitor path pushing/popping scopes exactly as Groovy's real scoping does (ScopeTrackingClassCodeExpressionTransformer lines 35-58 and 112-116). A misclassification in either direction means a property/attribute get or set on the `this` object (or the closure owner) is either falsely treated as harmless local access or routed through the CLOSURE_THIS asWritable().getOwner() hack, whose dynamic resolution the author explicitly calls unreliable. The comment at lines 254-263 states this hack is needed because 'Groovy doesn't seem to have any reliable way to do this'.
missing_evidence: StackVariableSet and ScopeTrackingClassCodeExpressionTransformer lines 121-179 (scope popping / visitClosureExpression handling) were not read.
A concrete script pattern where closure-owner resolution escapes the interceptor chain.
ClosureSupport.java and SandboxedMethodClosure.java were not readable in this session.
preconditions: Sandboxed code accesses an implicit-this property or variable inside or across a closure boundary where scope tracking and Groovy's actual resolution disagree.
The CLOSURE_THIS asWritable().getOwner() resolution picks a different object/target than intended.
candidates.title: Closure-scope heuristics (isLocalVariable / visitingClosureBody / CLOSURE_THIS) can misclassify dynamic access and skip property interception

counter_evidence: The code is explicitly labelled 'Apply SECURITY-582 fix to constructors' (line 157) and handles this(...), super(...) ordering (lines 183-192).
GroovyInterceptor.onSuperConstructor defaults to onNewInstance, so a filter overriding onNewInstance can still veto it (lines 55-57).
The interceptor is invoked via chain.next(), so a throwing interceptor aborts construction.
candidates.description: For classes whose superclass is not in TRIVIAL_CONSTRUCTORS (lines 151-162), processConstructors rewrites each constructor to (a) generate an auxiliary private constructor whose first statement calls the real super via scwArgs (lines 208-229) and (b) emit checkedSuperConstructor(superClass, args) before delegating with this(...) (lines 202-207). Checker.checkedSuperConstructor (lines 234-244) runs a VarArgInvokerChain and calls chain.next().onSuperConstructor(this, superClass, args) but ignores the result and unconditionally returns a new SuperConstructorWrapper(args); if the chain is empty it does nothing at all (no else branch, unlike checkedCall). GroovyInterceptor.onSuperConstructor (lines 55-57) by default forwards to onNewInstance, but a custom interceptor that expects to validate or veto the super construction receives a void-returning hook whose only veto is throwing. The wrapped-arg indirection ($scw.arg(i), lines 211-215) means the interceptor sees only wrapped indices rather than the evaluated super arguments, and the read source contains no check that the superclass constructor itself is legitimate. This is a design/robustness concern around the SECURITY-582 handling; the read source does not show a working bypass.
missing_evidence: Whether a real interceptor distinguishes onSuperConstructor from onNewInstance and what arguments it receives.
Any test or scenario demonstrating an unchecked superclass constructor effect.
preconditions: Sandboxed class extends a non-trivial superclass so the SECURITY-582 path is taken.
An interceptor that permits onSuperConstructor (e.g. forwards) is registered, allowing construction of that superclass.
candidates.title: super(...) constructor interception is chained through onSuperConstructor with no enforce in Checker

counter_evidence: GroovyValueFilter/README usage registers on the evaluating thread before shell.evaluate (README lines 28-31).
Lines 191-200 describe register()/reversal as an explicit lifecycle the host is expected to manage.
No evidence in the read set that sandboxed code can create threads while unchecked.
candidates.description: GroovyInterceptor.register() adds the interceptor to threadInterceptors.get() for the current thread (lines 194-196), and the class javadoc states the list is 'maintained per thread' (line 14). Consequently, checks only apply to threads that have an interceptor in scope. If sandboxed code causes execution on a different thread (a capability that itself depends on the interceptor policy), or if a host thread evaluates a script without first registering, no interceptor runs and Checker's fall-through paths (fakeCallSite etc.) execute operations unchecked. Combined with the fail-open fallback described in the first candidate, the security boundary is a per-thread, opt-in registration rather than a process-wide deny-by-default. The read source shows the registration mechanism but not how or whether it is inherited/propagated, so this is a scoping/robustness observation.
missing_evidence: Whether embedders propagate interceptors to child threads or install a global fallback.
The full threadInterceptors declaration and any ThreadLocal inheritance (source near lines 200-224 was not read).
preconditions: Script execution or a delegated call occurs on a thread where register() was not invoked (e.g. a spawned thread).
No global default-deny exists in the read code.
candidates.title: Interceptor registration is per-thread and inherited; a missing/mis-scoped registration silently disables all checks
